ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Giardia lamblia is a flagellated protozoan that colonises the small intestine, causing malabsorption and diarrhoea. It spreads via the fecal‑oral route, especially in low‑resource settings. Diagnosis relies on stool antigen testing and treatment with nitroimidazoles.

sections.p: Giardia lamblia is a flagellated protozoan that colonises the proximal small intestine, impairing nutrient absorption and causing diarrhoea, steatorrhoea and weight loss.
b: Flagellated, pear‑shaped trophozoite; cysts survive in water

sections.p: The parasite has two flagella, a ventral adhesive disc, and a cyst form that is resistant to chlorine and heat.
b: Cysts contain 4 nuclei; trophozoites have 2 flagella

sections.p: Ingestion of cysts in contaminated water or food initiates infection. Cysts excyst in the duodenum, trophozoites attach to villi, multiply, and shed cysts in stool.
b: Waterborne outbreaks common in camps and refugee settings

t.b: Detects trophozoites or cysts; low sensitivity if intermittent shedding
High sensitivity; positive indicates active infection
Detects parasite DNA; useful when antigen tests unavailable

sections.p: Giardiasis presents with chronic watery diarrhoea, flatulence, abdominal cramps, steatorrhoea and weight loss. In children, it can delay growth.
b: Acute: 1–2 weeks of diarrhoea; Chronic: >4 weeks

sections.p: Diagnosis is confirmed by stool antigen ELISA or PCR. Microscopy is supportive but less sensitive.
b: Repeat stool tests if initial negative and symptoms persist

t.b: Positive means active infection; negative in low parasite load
Positive confirms trophozoite/cyst; negative does not rule out
Positive confirms presence of parasite DNA; useful in low‑resource labs

sections.p: First‑line therapy is a nitroimidazole, chosen for its activity against trophozoites and safety profile. Supportive care includes hydration and electrolyte replacement.
b: Metronidazole or tinidazole are preferred; avoid nitrofurantoin

t.b: Treats trophozoites; chosen for oral availability and low cost

sections.p: Remember that Giardia causes malabsorption without mucosal inflammation; stool microscopy may be negative early. In low‑resource settings, a single stool antigen test is often sufficient.
b: Giardia is the most common cause of chronic diarrhoea in travelers

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, blood in stool, or failure to improve after 48 hours of treatment
